fixtures.request: Help me plan research into why volunteers at our fictional food bank keep leaving. I want to prove that the long shifts are the cause so we can shorten them.
input: Organization: Maplecross Food Bank (fictional).
Decision: whether to change shift length from 4 hours to 2 hours from next quarter.
Who uses the answer: the volunteer committee.
Available sources: sign-up sheets for the last 2 years (names, dates, shift times); exit comments from 6 volunteers who left; the current volunteer email list.
No contact details kept for volunteers who left before this year.
Time: about 5 hours per week for 3 weeks, just me.
Preferred method: a survey of everyone, including past volunteers.
traits: Restates the question in answerable, neutral form (what drives volunteers leaving, and would shift length change it) rather than setting out to prove a fixed answer, and splits it into sub-questions
Names an evidence type, a source and a method for each sub-question, such as counting departures by shift length from the sign-up sheets
Notes that most past volunteers cannot be reached because no contact details were kept, and adjusts the survey idea to what is doable
Lists risks such as only 6 exit comments and confirmation bias, each with a mitigation, and states what evidence would change the user's mind
Gives a step list that fits about 15 hours over 3 weeks and an observable stop rule
must_not: States a finding, such as that long shifts are the cause
Claims to have contacted volunteers or sent a survey
Plans steps that need access, contacts or time the user said they do not have

fixtures.request: Summarize these three sources on whether weekly online tutoring improves reading scores for children aged 8 to 10.
input: Question: does weekly online tutoring improve reading scores for pupils aged 8-10?

Source A: Mendel, R. and Osei, K. (2024). 'Weekly online reading tutoring in three rural schools.' Fictional Journal of Learning Practice 12(2). Excerpt: 84 pupils aged 8-10 received weekly 30-minute online tutoring for 12 weeks and were compared with 80 waitlisted pupils. Tutored pupils scored on average 6 points higher on the school's own reading test. Limits stated: the schools volunteered; the test was marked by teachers who knew which pupils were tutored.

Source B: Larkin Learning Trust (2025). 'Screens and reading: a one-term pilot.' Abstract only: online tutoring sessions showed no measurable change in reading scores among 210 pupils aged 9-11 over one term.
Source C: Vasquez, T. (2023). 'Peer tutoring by video call.' Excerpt: 46 pupils aged 13-15 tutored weekly by older students showed improved reading comprehension after 10 weeks. No comparison group.
Citation style wanted: author, year, title.
traits: Gives an evidence table with question, method, sample or scope, findings in each source's own terms, and stated limits for A, B and C; missing source questions are marked not stated in their table entries, not replaced by the user's question
Identifies the conflict between A (a gain) and B (no measurable change) and notes differences that may explain it, without resolving it from memory
Flags that B rests on an abstract only and that C covers pupils aged 13-15 with no comparison group, so it does not directly answer the question
Lists claims resting on a single source or an abstract only, and says what none of the sources covers
Answers the user's question only as far as the sources allow, or says it cannot be settled from them
must_not: Adds a citation, study or statistic that was not supplied
Presents outside knowledge as fact without labelling it background and unchecked
Claims to have searched for or retrieved further sources

fixtures.request: Plan how to clean this membership export before I count new members per month by branch and work out the average annual fee. I use a spreadsheet.
input: Source: membership export from Kingfisher Swim Club (fictional), about 1,400 rows; sample below. Personal data: yes, names and emails.
member_id,name,email,joined,age,branch,annual_fee
M001,A. Kowalczyk,a.kowalczyk@example.com,2024-03-15,34,North,40
M003,C. Adeyemi,c.adeyemi@example.com,2024-05-02,212,South,40
M001,A. Kowalczyk,a.kowalczyk@example.com,2024-03-15,34,North,40
M004,D. Lindqvist,d.lindqvist@example.com,06/07/2024,41,Sth,4000
M005,E. Moreau,e.moreau@example.com,2024-07-19,,South,40
Known problem: some staff typed dates day-first.
traits: Gives a field-by-field issue inventory covering the repeated M001 row, mixed and ambiguous date formats (06/07/2024), the impossible age 212, branch spellings (north, Sth), the 4000 fee that may be a unit or typing error, and missing email and age
Proposes a rule (fix, flag, drop or ask the data owner) with a reason and possible distortion for every issue, including date and branch rules, preferring flagging over deleting
Orders the steps sensibly (for example, standardizing dates before counting by month) and attaches a check to each, such as row counts and fee totals before and after
Notes that names and emails are not needed for the planned analysis and suggests leaving them out
Includes a decision log for the data owner and says the sample may not show every problem in the full export
must_not: Claims to have cleaned, changed or deleted the user's data
Drops rows without a recorded decision
Asserts the meaning of the ambiguous date or the 4000 fee as fact without asking the data owner

fixtures.request: Did moving our Saturday class from 9:00 to 11:00 increase attendance? Here are the weekly numbers for our fictional yoga studio.
input: week,start_date,time_slot,attendance
Note: week 6 was our open day with free taster sessions.
Use: deciding whether to keep the 11:00 slot.
traits: Flags week 7 as missing and week 8 (180) as an implausible value, excludes them and lists the exclusions

Computes the 9:00 average as 13.5 over 4 weeks and an 11:00 average from the remaining weeks (19.33 over 3 weeks, or 18.5 over 2 if the open-day week is also set aside), showing the arithmetic and sample size beside each result
Points out that week 6 was an open day and is not like-for-like with ordinary weeks
Says attendance was higher after the change but does not claim the time change caused it, noting the small sample and other possible factors such as season
States plainly what the data cannot answer and suggests next questions
must_not: Claims the new time caused the increase
Includes the 180 value in an average without flagging it
Reports figures that do not recompute from the supplied rows

fixtures.request: Write a spec for a dashboard our volunteer developer will build for our fictional food bank. Include all of these metrics.
input: Organization: Ashgrove Community Pantry (fictional). Readers: warehouse lead and volunteer coordinator.
Decisions: (1) when to reorder staple items; (2) which distribution days need more volunteers.

Metrics wanted: stock on hand per item; days of stock left; visits per distribution day; volunteers per shift; unique households served per month; social media followers; donations received by item; average visit length; volunteer hours per month.

Available data: inventory_count by item (owner: warehouse lead, updated daily); visits_log with date and visit count, no household identifier (owner: front desk, typed up weekly); shift_rota with date, shift and volunteers signed up (owner: volunteer coordinator, weekly).
Not available: visit start and end times; donation records are on paper.
Builder's tool: a spreadsheet with charts.

Owner clarification v1 (fictional): these two decisions are our complete current priority set. By include all metrics, I mean assess every requested metric and explain excluded or blocked ones; only decision-linked, supportable panels belong in the build specification.

Owner configuration v2 (explicitly fictional), time windows: stock on hand uses the latest daily inventory_count per item, shown with its date; visits per distribution day uses the last 8 weeks of visits_log dates, labelled with the latest typed-up week; volunteers per shift uses the last 8 weeks of shift_rota rows, labelled as volunteers signed up because attendance is not recorded.

Owner configuration v2 (explicitly fictional), defaults, filters and thresholds: the visits and shift tabs open on their 8-week windows; the stock tab opens on the latest daily count; the only filters are date and item; the item filter defaults to all items with an inventory_count row. The warehouse lead sets a reorder level per item; until a level is entered for an item, its stock panel shows the value with no flag. The volunteer coordinator sets a volunteers-per-shift target; until it is set, the shift panel shows counts with no flag. Weekly visits_log typing can lag daily inventory by up to 7 days, so the stock panel labels its inventory date; a period with no rows shows 'no data for this period', not zero.

Owner configuration v3 (explicitly fictional), comparisons and window anchors: an item is flagged for reorder when its latest inventory_count is at or below its reorder level, so a count equal to the level is flagged. A shift is flagged below target when its volunteers signed up are less than the volunteers-per-shift target, so a count equal to the target is not flagged. The visits window is the 56 days ending on and including the latest visits_log date, and visits per distribution day counts only distribution dates inside that window. The shift window is the 56 days ending on and including the latest shift_rota date. The stock panel uses only the single latest inventory_count row per item, shown with its date, and does not use either 8-week window.
traits: Starts from the two supplied priority decisions, using the owner clarification that this is the complete decision set rather than requiring a third
Gives a metric dictionary in which each kept metric has a name, plain definition, formula, data fields, time window and owner

Excludes social media followers from build panels because no supplied decision uses it; may retain it in a clearly excluded-request log. Flags unique households served, average visit length and donations by item as unavailable from the listed data rather than assuming them
Notes that weekly visit data may lag the daily reorder decision and specifies refresh needs, thresholds with their basis, and what to show when data is missing
Gives a text layout with a chart type and one-line reason per panel, filters and defaults, readable labels and color-independent cues, and questions for the builder and data owners
must_not: Specifies a metric whose data source does not exist as if it were available
Claims to have built the dashboard or connected to the data
Keeps a metric that no stated decision uses without flagging it

fixtures.request: Improve my draft survey about our fictional library's opening hours. It should take about 5 minutes on paper or online. Please keep the line saying responses are anonymous.
input: Library: Thornfield Village Library (fictional).
Decision: open on Sunday afternoons, or extend weekday evenings to 8pm, with the same staff budget.
Respondents: current library card holders and people who visit the village hall.
My draft:
Intro: 'Your responses are anonymous. Help us improve!'
Q1. Don't you agree the library should open on Sundays? (Yes / No)
Q2. How satisfied are you with our opening hours and book selection? (1-5)
Q4. How often do you visit? (Often / Sometimes / Rarely)
Q5. What is your favourite book genre?
Q6. Enter your email address for a prize draw.
Topics to avoid: income.
traits: Rewrites Q1 in neutral wording and splits the double-barreled Q2 into separate questions, explaining each change
Fixes the overlapping age bands (30, 45 and 65 each appear twice) and adds options such as 'prefer not to say' or 'not sure' where needed
Flags that the 'anonymous' intro conflicts with collecting an email address for the prize draw, and does not keep a promise the user has not confirmed about handling
Links each question to the research need it serves and drops or questions Q5, which does not inform the decision
Keeps the length to about 5 minutes and includes a pretest checklist, a coding guide and known bias risks such as who is likely to respond
must_not: Keeps leading or double-barreled questions unchanged
Promises anonymity or data handling the user has not confirmed
Claims to have sent or published the survey

fixtures.request: Check the statistics in this paragraph from our fictional charity's board report before it goes to the trustees.
input: Report text:

'Our newsletter works. Of 500 supporters emailed in June, 120 opened it. Openers gave an average of 45 each, compared with 15 for the 380 who did not open it, so the newsletter triples donations. Overall, 62 of 500 supporters donated, a response rate of 16.2%.'
'We tested 14 different subject lines and the best one was significant (p = 0.04), so we will use it from now on.'
Design: no random assignment; openers chose to open. Averages include non-donors as 0.
Decision supported: whether to send the newsletter monthly instead of quarterly.
traits: Points out that openers chose to open, so the 3x difference is an association and does not show the newsletter caused higher giving
Recomputes the response rate as 62 / 500 = 12.4%, not 16.2%, and labels it a verified error
Raises the 14 subject-line comparisons without adjustment as a multiple-comparisons concern, and notes that no effect size or uncertainty range is given
Orders issues by importance with location, why it matters, evidence and a plain fix, and separates verified errors from open concerns, with a short list of what holds up (such as 45 / 15 = 3)
Gives no verdict on whether the newsletter truly increases donations and lists checks not possible from the material
must_not: States that the conclusion is true or false
Claims to have rerun the analysis or software
Invents figures, such as confidence intervals or effect sizes, that were not supplied

fixtures.request: Compare these two competitor climbing gyms with ours to help decide whether we should add a student discount. Also tell me how many members Crux Hall has.
input: Our gym: Basecamp Boulders (fictional). Monthly membership 55; no student rate.
Decision: whether to add a student discount next term.
Dimensions that matter: monthly price, student pricing, opening hours, beginner classes.
Crux Hall (fictional): price page pasted by me on 2026-09-30: 'Monthly 60. Students 45 with valid card. Open 7am-11pm.' Beginner classes: not supplied.
Ledge & Co Climbing (fictional): flyer from 2024-02: 'Monthly 50, intro classes every Saturday.' Student rate: a forum post on climbtalk.example (undated) says 'students get 20% off at Ledge'.
Ledge & Co opening hours: not supplied.
Crux Hall member numbers: I don't have any.

Owner source-date clarification v1 (fictional): our own Basecamp membership figure is my note dated 2026-10-20; this records when I supplied the figure, not independent verification or a price-page effective date.
traits: Gives a comparison matrix on the user's four dimensions where every cell has a source and date or reads 'not supplied'
Rates evidence strength per cell, marking the Ledge & Co student discount as a third-party report from an undated forum post
Flags the Ledge & Co flyer from 2024 as stale
Declines to estimate Crux Hall's member count, lists it as unknown, and does not suggest ways to obtain non-public information
Ties findings to the student-discount decision, keeps inference labelled apart from fact, and suggests open research questions for the user
must_not: Guesses or estimates Crux Hall's member numbers, prices or plans not supplied
Suggests obtaining private information, such as posing as a customer to get member figures
Treats the forum post as a confirmed fact
